passages.title: Diverted by accumulation until the graves
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah al-Takāthur 1–2

**What this passage is about.** In two short lines Allah names the thing that quietly consumes a human life — the race to have *more* — and then tells us exactly where that race ends. Ayah 1 diagnoses: something has diverted you. Ayah 2 gives the terminus: the diversion runs until you are in the graveyard. The two ayat hold together as a single sentence — a distraction and the point at which it stops — and their force comes from the fact that nothing interrupts the race along the way. No word here says "then you woke up." The competition simply runs on until the earth closes over it.

## "Diverted" — a word for a life spent elsewhere

The opening verb, *alhākum*, is not the language of forbidding. Allah does not say "amassing wealth is unlawful." He says it *diverted* you. Ibn Kathir gives the sense directly: people are preoccupied by love of the world, its delights and its adornments, and this distracts them from seeking the Hereafter and from desiring it.

That is the whole tragedy in one word. The wealth is not accused; the person is. The thing that occupied you was never the point of your existence, and while you were occupied, the actual point went unattended.

Notice too the breadth of the address. Ibn Kathir opens his comment with it: Allah says that **all** are preoccupied by love of the world. The verse does not point at a class of villains. It points at a crowd, and the reader is standing in it.

## *Takāthur*: the race, not the riches

Everything in ayah 1 turns on the word *al-takāthur*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that it is derived from the root *kathrah* and means "to amass much wealth" — the interpretation assigned to it by Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās and Ḥasan al-Baṣrī.

Qatādah adds a second shade of meaning: the word is also used in the sense of **taking pride in the abundance of material goods**. So *takāthur* is not merely having a lot. It carries the *more-than-you* instinct: piling up in order to be seen piling up. The renderings in front of us catch that flavour — "competition for more," "the mutual increase" — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān later describes the condition plainly as people "racing each other in wealth and children." A race requires a rival.

**And what, concretely, is being blamed?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān preserves a precious report here: Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās reports that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited this verse and explained its meaning as **"Acquiring wealth but not paying out of it the obligatory dues"** (transmitted via Qurṭubī). That is a mercy of a definition. The condemnation is not aimed at the existence of property, but at property held with its rights withheld — wealth that comes in and never goes out to the one who has a claim on it.

## The Prophet's ﷺ own words — so close to revelation that the Companions were unsure

The single most striking thing in the sources on ayah 1 is a report Ibn Kathir cites from **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī**, in the *Book of ar-Riqāq* (the narrations that soften the heart), from Anas bin Mālik, that **Ubayy bin Kaʿb** said:

> "We used to think that this was a part of the Qur'an until the ayah was revealed which says: *Alhākum al-takāthur*."

What was "this"? Ibn Kathir explains that Ubayy was referring to the ḥadīth in which the Prophet ﷺ said: *"If the Son of Adam had a valley of gold, he would desire another like it…"* — and there Ibn Kathir leaves the wording short.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the saying at greater length, recording it from **Imām Bukhārī, from Sayyidnā Anas**, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> **"If the Son of Adam has a valley of gold, he would love to have two valleys, and nothing but the dust of grave will fill his mouth. And Allah accepts the repentance of him who turns to Him in penitence."**

Sit with what Ubayy bin Kaʿb is telling us. These words were so weighty that senior Companions carried them for a time believing they were Qur'an. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains how this happened: it seems the Prophet ﷺ recited the verse and interpreted it in his own words, so some of the Companions were under the impression that the Prophetic words were part of the Qur'an. Later, when the sūrah was recited in its entirety and those words were not in it, they realised that his ﷺ words were explanatory — a commentary on the verse, not a part of it.

So we possess the Messenger's ﷺ own gloss on *takāthur*, and it moves in three steps:

1. **The appetite is self-multiplying.** A valley of gold does not satisfy; it produces the wish for a second valley. Whatever number you had in mind was never the number.
2. **Only the grave closes the mouth.** "Nothing but the dust of grave will fill his mouth" — the craving has exactly one cure, and it is not acquisition. This is precisely the bridge into ayah 2.
3. **The door is open.** "And Allah accepts the repentance of him who turns to Him in penitence." The saying does not end in despair. The same breath that exposes the appetite offers the way out.

## "My wealth, my wealth" — auditing what you actually own

Imām Aḥmad records from **ʿAbdullāh bin ash-Shikhkhīr** that he came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he was reciting *Alhākum al-takāthur* and saying:

> **"The Son of Adam says, 'My wealth, my wealth.' But do you get anything of benefit from your wealth except that which you ate and finished, or that which you clothed yourself with and wore out, or that which you gave as charity and have spent?"**

Ibn Kathir notes that Muslim, at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʼī also recorded this ḥadīth. And Muslim records in his Ṣaḥīḥ from Abū Hurayrah a version with a closing line that lands like a door shutting:

> **"The servant says, 'My wealth, my wealth.' Yet he only gets three benefits from his wealth: that which he eats and finishes, that which he wears until it is worn out, or that which he gives in charity and it is spent. Everything else other than that will go away and leave him for the people."**

Ibn Kathir observes that Muslim was alone in recording this ḥadīth.

Look closely at the audit. Of the three things that are genuinely "yours," two are already gone by definition — food consumed, clothing worn to threads. Only the third survives its own spending. Charity is the one form of expenditure that does not empty you. Everything else on the balance sheet, the Prophet ﷺ says, "will go away and leave him for the people" — it changes owner the moment you do. The possessive pronoun in "my wealth" turns out to be the emptiest word in the sentence.

## Ayah 2: "until you visit the graves"

*Ḥattā zurtum al-maqābir* is rendered before us as "until you visit the graves" — the language of paying a visit. Ibn Kathir explains what the diversion actually costs: *this delays you until death comes to you and you visit the graves, thus becoming its inhabitants.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to close off any misreading: "reaching the graves" here means **to die and be buried in them** — this is not about strolling through a cemetery. And it cites the Prophet's ﷺ own explanation of this very verse, that it means *"until death overtakes you"* (reported via Ibn Kathir, from Ibn Abī Ḥātim).

Then Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the implication of the two ayat read together: many people are engrossed in acquiring worldly goods and racing each other in wealth and children and the rest, and remain neglectful of the Hereafter until death comes upon them.

Feel the shape of the sentence. Ayah 1 sets a process running; ayah 2 supplies the only thing that stops it, and it is not a change of heart — it is a burial. The race has no natural finish line inside this life. Whatever you told yourself you were racing *toward*, the verse tells you where you were actually heading the whole time.

## What comes with you, and what turns back

Al-Bukhārī records from Anas bin Mālik that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> **"Three things follow the deceased person, and two of them return while one remains behind with him. The things which follow him are his family, his wealth and his deeds. His family and his wealth return while his deeds remain."**

Ibn Kathir notes this ḥadīth was also recorded by Muslim, at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʼī.

This is the funeral procession described from the graveside. Everything *takāthur* worked for walks with you to the edge of the pit — and then walks home. Only your deeds go down with you. The two ayat and this ḥadīth are saying the same thing from two directions: you spent a lifetime accumulating what is bound to turn back at the graveyard gate.

**And the appetite does not weaken with age.** Imām Aḥmad records from Anas that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> **"The Son of Adam becomes old with senility, but yet two things remain with him: greed and hope."**

Ibn Kathir notes that both al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded this ḥadīth in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs. This is why ayah 2 says *until the graves* and not "until you have had enough." Waiting for the hunger to subside on its own is waiting for something the Prophet ﷺ told us does not happen. Whatever is going to break the diversion has to be a decision, not the passage of time.

## Living it

The sources point to something narrower and more doable than a vague call to detachment:

- **Pay what is owed.** The Prophet's ﷺ explanation of the verse, reported by Ibn ʿAbbās, targets wealth acquired without paying out of it the obligatory dues. Begin there.
- **Move things from column two into column three.** Of the three benefits Muslim records — eaten, worn out, given away — only the given-away one outlives you. Every act of charity is a transfer from the wealth that "will go away and leave him for the people" into the deeds that "remain."
- **Compete over something else.** Qatādah's shade of *takāthur* — taking pride in the abundance of material goods — suggests the honest question is not only "how much do I have?" but "who am I trying to out-have?"
- **Repent; the door is open.** The saying reported from Imām Bukhārī, from Anas, that exposes the valley of gold ends: *"And Allah accepts the repentance of him who turns to Him in penitence."*

## A note on the sūrah's weight

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits (from Mazharī, with reference to Ḥākim and Bayhaqī, on the authority of Ibn ʿUmar) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is reported to have once asked the noble Companions whether anyone among them had the strength to recite a thousand verses a day. They replied, "Who can recite a thousand verses a day?" He ﷺ said, "Can you not recite Sūrah at-Takāthur?" — which implies that this short sūrah equals in weight and worth a thousand verses.

Eight brief ayat, and the first two of them have already located you: mid-race, and nearer the end of it than you think. The mercy of ayat 1 and 2 is that they arrive while there is still time to stop running.

passages.title: The twice-repeated threat and the knowledge you refuse
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is doing

After telling us in ayat 1–2 that the race to outdo one another kept us busy right up to the graves, Allah now interrupts. Three times in a row He begins with **كَلَّا — "But no!"** — and twice He follows it with the same warning: *you shall come to know*. Ayat 3–5 are that interruption: a threat, the identical threat repeated, and then a third rebuke that turns the accusation inward — the problem is not that you lack information about death and accountability, it is that you do not *know* it in the way knowledge deserves to be known.

What holds the three ayat together is a single word repeated in every one of them: **تَعْلَمُونَ — "you know."** Ayah 3: you shall come to know. Ayah 4: again, you shall come to know. Ayah 5: if only you knew, with sure knowledge. The passage is about knowledge — the knowledge coming toward you whether you want it or not, and the knowledge you are refusing right now.

---

## "But no!" — the word that cuts the sentence off

Every one of these three ayat opens with **كَلَّا**. The renderings give it as "But no!", "Again, no!", "Nay!" It is a word of arrest. The previous two ayat described people absorbed in competing and accumulating — and this word breaks in and stops the sentence.

Notice what it does *not* say. It does not argue with them. It does not present evidence. It simply refuses the whole posture: no, this is not how things are, and you are about to find out.

## Ayah 3 and ayah 4: the same words, twice

Look at the two ayat side by side in the Arabic:

> **كَلَّا سَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ**
> **ثُمَّ كَلَّا سَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ**

They are word-for-word identical except for one addition at the front of the second: **ثُمَّ**, "then / again." Allah says the same thing twice, and the only new element is a word meaning *and after that*.

**Al-Hasan Al-Basri** said of the two together: *"This is a threat after a threat."* The repetition is not decoration. It is the second blow of a hammer on the same nail.

**Ad-Dahhak** read the repetition differently, taking the two addresses as aimed at two audiences: the first — *"Nay! You shall come to know!"* — meaning *O you disbelievers*; and the second — *"Again nay! You shall come to know!"* — meaning *O you believers*. On his reading, no one gets to stand outside this warning. The disbeliever will come to know, and so will the believer.

Both sayings are transmitted by Ibn Kathir, one after the other, without him ruling either out, and the reader can hold both. Al-Hasan's reading gives you the force of the repetition; Ad-Dahhak's gives you its reach. If Ad-Dahhak is right, then the believer who assumes this surah is describing somebody else has just been named in ayah 4.

**"You shall *soon* come to know."** The verb carries the particle **سَوْفَ**, which the renderings give as "will soon" or "shall." The threat is not conditional and it is not left as a possibility. What Allah leaves unstated is only the timing.

## What exactly will you come to know?

The Qur'an does not leave the threat abstract. **Ibn Kathir** points out that the ayat which follow this passage — *"Verily, you shall see the blazing Fire! And again, you shall see it with certainty of sight!"* — are, in his words, "the explanation of the previous threat" of ayat 3 and 4. That is the content of *you shall come to know*: **sight of the Fire**.

"Thus," Ibn Kathir writes, "Allah threatens them with this situation, which is what the people of the Fire will see. It is a Fire, which if it exhaled one breath, every angel who is near (to Allah) and every Prophet who was sent would all fall down on their knees due to fear, awe and the sight of its horrors." He immediately adds that this is "based upon what has been reported in the narrations concerning it" — he is passing on transmitted material, not speculating.

Sit with the proportion in that image. Not the sinner brought to the edge of it — the angels brought near to Allah, and the Prophets who were sent. One breath of that Fire, and *they* fall to their knees. And the people being warned here are busy tallying who has more.

## Ayah 5: the sentence Allah did not finish

The third **كَلَّا** changes direction:

> **كَلَّا لَوْ تَعْلَمُونَ عِلْمَ الْيَقِينِ**
> *"Nay! If you knew with a sure knowledge."*

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** draws attention to something a reader in English can easily walk past. The Arabic word **لَوْ**, "if," opens a conditional sentence — and in Arabic, as in English, an "if" clause needs a main clause to complete it: *if you knew... then what?* In the commentary's words, "the word 'if' requires a principal clause that seems missing here."

The commentary explains that the context supplies what the words leave unsaid: *"If you had the sure knowledge of accountability on the Day of Judgment, you would not have engrossed yourselves in mutual competition in acquiring worldly goods and taking pride in their abundance."*

**Ibn Kathir** fills the gap in almost the same terms: *"if you knew with true knowledge, you would not be diverted by rivalry for wealth away from seeking the abode of the Hereafter until you reach the graves."*

Both scholars, then, complete the sentence by pointing straight back at ayat 1–2. The unfinished condition is a mirror: *if you really knew, you would not be living like this.* And there is a rhetorical mercy in leaving it unfinished. A sentence you have to complete yourself is a sentence you cannot read at a distance.

## "Sure knowledge"

The phrase **عِلْمَ الْيَقِينِ** — rendered "sure knowledge" by both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān — is the hinge of the whole passage. It tells you that the failure being diagnosed is not ignorance in the ordinary sense.

Everyone being addressed here already knows that people die; ayah 2 has already brought them to the graves. They know, as a fact filed somewhere in the mind, that there is a reckoning. What ayah 5 says is that this is not yet **sure knowledge** — knowing of the kind that reaches conduct. On both commentators' reading, real knowledge would have pulled them out of the race. Since the race continues, the knowledge is not real.

And notice the wording of the surah itself. Ayah 5 speaks of *sure knowledge*, **عِلْمَ الْيَقِينِ**; ayah 7 will speak of **عَيْنَ الْيَقِينِ**, "certainty of sight" — seeing it with your own eyes. Knowing, and then seeing.

That is why ayat 3 and 4 say *you **shall** come to know*. The coming to know is guaranteed either way.

## What the Prophet ﷺ taught alongside these words

The narrations Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān bring for this surah are all, in effect, illustrations of the gap between what we think we know about our wealth and what is actually true of it.

**Imam Ahmad** recorded from 'Abdullah bin Ash-Shikhkhir that he came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he was reciting *"The mutual increase diverts you"* and saying:

> *"The Son of Adam says, 'My wealth, my wealth.' But do you get anything (of benefit) from your wealth except for that which you ate and you finished it, or that which you clothed yourself with and you wore it out, or that which you gave as charity and you have spent it?"*

Ibn Kathir notes that Muslim, At-Tirmidhi and An-Nasa'i also recorded this hadith. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing this same report, adds a further clause from a narration by Muslim: *"Everything else other than that will go away, and he will leave it for other people"* — that is, the commentary glosses, for his inheritors.

Separately, **Muslim** recorded in his *Sahih* from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> *"The servant says 'My wealth, my wealth.' Yet he only gets three (benefits) from his wealth: that which he eats and finishes, that which he wears until it is worn out, or that which he gives in charity and it is spent. Everything else other than that will go away and leave him for the people."*

Ibn Kathir notes that Muslim was alone in recording this one.

Notice the strangeness of the accounting. Of a lifetime's wealth, what is genuinely *yours* is only what has already been consumed, worn out, or given away — and the rest goes away and is left behind for other people.

**Al-Bukhari** recorded from Anas bin Malik that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> *"Three things follow the deceased person, and two of them return while one remains behind with him. The things which follow him are his family, his wealth and his deeds. His family and his wealth return while his deeds remain."*

This hadith was also recorded by Muslim, At-Tirmidhi and An-Nasa'i. It is a picture of the very moment ayah 2 arrived at — and it shows what *you shall come to know* will look like: the crowd walking back, and you left with the one thing you were least busy about.

**Imam Ahmad** recorded from Anas that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"The Son of Adam becomes old with senility, but yet two things remain with him: greed and hope."*

Ibn Kathir notes that both Al-Bukhari and Muslim recorded this hadith in the Two Sahihs. This is the diagnosis behind ayah 5. The appetite that ayat 1–2 describe does not fade with age — it outlasts strength itself. That is why the correction has to come from outside, in the form of a *kallā*.

## The words the Companions took for Qur'an

**Ibn Kathir** reports that in *Sahih Al-Bukhari*, in the Book of Ar-Riqaq (the narrations that soften the heart), it is recorded from Anas bin Malik that Ubayy bin Ka'b said: *"We used to think that this was a part of the Qur'an until the Ayah was revealed which says, 'The mutual increase diverts you.'"* Ubayy was referring, Ibn Kathir says, to the hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ said, *"If the Son of Adam had a valley of gold, he would desire another like it..."* — and there Ibn Kathir's quotation of the hadith's wording breaks off.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** cites that hadith at greater length, reporting that Imam Bukhari records from Sayyidna Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> *"If the Son of 'Adam has a valley of gold, he would love to have two valleys, and nothing but the dust of grave will fill his mouth. And Allah accepts the repentance of him who turns to Him in penitence."*

The commentary then reports Ubayy Ibn Ka'b's remark about this same tradition and explains what happened: it seems the Prophet ﷺ recited the ayah and interpreted it in his own words, and some of the Companions were under the impression that his words were part of the revelation; later, when the surah was recited in its entirety and those words were not in it, they realised the Prophetic words were explanatory rather than Qur'an.

And note where that hadith ends. Even in a narration about an appetite that nothing but the dust of the grave will fill, the door is left open: *Allah accepts the repentance of him who turns to Him in penitence.*

---

## Living it

**Treat this as addressed to you.** On Ad-Dahhak's reading, ayah 4 is the believer's copy of the same warning. Anyone who reads ayat 3–5 and pictures somebody else has missed the ayah.

**Test your knowledge by your calendar, not your beliefs.** Ayah 5's unfinished sentence is a diagnostic tool that both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān hand you: *if you really had sure knowledge, you would not be spending yourself on rivalry.* So look at what your weeks are actually organised around. Ibn Kathir's phrase is precise — being "diverted by rivalry for wealth away from seeking the abode of the Hereafter." The problem is not owning things. It is competing.

**Convert what you can while conversion is still possible.** The accounting the Prophet ﷺ gave leaves one category of wealth that stays with you. Family and wealth return from the graveside; deeds remain.

**Keep the door in view.** The same narration that describes an appetite only the grave will fill ends by saying that Allah accepts the repentance of whoever turns to Him. Ayat 3 and 4 do not say *you might* come to know. They say *you shall*, twice. The mercy of the whole passage is that Allah says it now, while there is still time between the warning and the sight.

passages.title: Seeing the Fire, then answering for the blessings
passages.tafsir:
**In one breath:** after warning twice that "you shall come to know," Allah now tells the heedless exactly *what* they will come to know — they will see the Fire, and then they will stand and answer for the good things they were given. Ayat 6–7 turn the earlier threat into a scene; ayah 8 turns the scene into a personal questioning. What holds the three together is a single movement: from being told, to seeing, to being asked.

## The threat finally made explicit

Ibn Kathīr reads these ayat as the direct completion of what came before. Earlier the surah had said only, *"Nay! You shall come to know! Again nay! You shall come to know!"* — a warning with the content left blank. Al-Ḥasan Al-Baṣrī commented on that pair simply: "This is a threat after a threat." Then came the unfinished sentence, *"Nay! If you knew with a sure knowledge,"* which Ibn Kathīr completes: if you knew with true knowledge, you would not be diverted by rivalry for wealth away from seeking the abode of the Hereafter until you reach the graves.

And now, says Ibn Kathīr, ayat 6–7 are "the explanation of the previous threat." The blank is filled in. What is it that you shall come to know? *"Verily, you shall see the blazing Fire! And again you shall see it with certainty of sight!"* Everything the surah has been circling — the mutual increase, the rivalry for wealth, the graves — arrives here, at a sight.

## Seeing, not merely hearing: ʿayn al-yaqīn

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the key phrase of ayah 7 directly: *ʿayn al-yaqīn*, rendered "the eye of certainty" or "certainty of sight," "refers to the certainty attained by physical observation, and this is the highest degree of certainty."

To show what that means in practice, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates a report from Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him). When the Prophet Mūsā (peace be upon him) was on the mount of Ṭūr, his people began worshipping a calf. Allah informed him of it while he was still on the mountain — yet this piece of information did not affect him so much. But when he returned and saw the Children of Israel with his own eyes worshipping the calf, he became so indignant that the tablets of the Torah involuntarily fell from his hands. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes this as transmitted by Aḥmad and Ṭabarānī with an authentic chain of narrators, as quoted by Maẓharī.)

That is the point being pressed on the reader. Mūsā (peace be upon him) received the news from Allah Himself — the most reliable report conceivable — and still, *seeing* struck differently. So what of a person who has spent a lifetime hearing about the Fire and half-listening, and then one day sees it?

Notice too the repetition across ayat 6 and 7. Ayah 6 says you will surely see it; ayah 7 says again, you will surely see it — with the eye of certainty. The Qurʼān is not so much adding information the second time as refusing to let the reader move on.

## What the sight is

Ibn Kathīr does not describe the Fire at length. He says that Allah threatens them here with the situation "which is what the people of the Fire will see," and then offers one image: it is a Fire which, if it exhaled one breath, every angel who is near to Allah and every Prophet who was sent would all fall down on their knees due to fear, awe and the sight of its horrors. He adds that this is based upon what has been reported in the narrations concerning it, without naming a collection — so we take it exactly as he gives it, an image transmitted rather than a hadith we can attribute to a book.

Sit with the proportion for a moment. The surah began with people preoccupied by love of the world, its delights and its adornments — with the son of Adam saying "My wealth, my wealth." It ends up in front of something whose mere exhalation would bring the greatest of creation to their knees. The whole scale of the opening rivalry collapses.

## Ayah 8: and then the questioning

*"Then on that Day you shall be asked about the delights!"*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the same words: "Then you will be asked about all the pleasures [you enjoyed in the world]." Here the surah does something more searching than describing punishment: it hands the reader a bill.

Ibn Kathīr gives the meaning plainly: on that Day you all will be questioned concerning your gratitude towards the favours that Allah blessed you with, "such as health, safety, sustenance and other things." The question is not merely *did you have these things*, but "did you return His favours by being thankful to Him and worshipping Him." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the same question in two directions: had you shown gratitude towards Allah's favours, or did you misuse them and were ungrateful to Allah?

**How wide is the question?** Mujāhid — described by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as the leading authority on tafsīr — said that this questioning relates to every delight of the world a person enjoyed, whether in connection with food, clothes, house, wife, children, kingdom, government or honour. Qurṭubī, having cited this, concludes that it is absolutely true, and gives the reason from the wording itself: the question does not specify any particular blessing. Nothing, therefore, is excluded.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also points to another ayah where some of these favours are named explicitly: *"Surely, the ear, the eye and the heart — each one of them shall be interrogated about"* (17:36). These organs and their faculties comprehend millions of blessings of Allah, and a person will be questioned as to how he used them at every moment of his life.

## From the Sunnah

The commentaries anchor ayah 8 in several narrations, and one of them is a whole small story — worth telling properly, because it shows just how ordinary a "delight" can be.

**The dates and the sheep.** Ibn Jarīr records, through his chain, from Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that Abū Bakr and ʿUmar were sitting when the Prophet ﷺ came to them and asked, *"What has caused you two to sit here?"* They replied: "By He Who has sent you with the truth, nothing has brought us out of our houses except hunger." The Prophet ﷺ said, *"By He Who has sent me with the truth, nothing has brought me out other than this."*

So they went until they came to the house of a man from the Anṣār, and the woman of the house received them. The Prophet ﷺ asked her where her husband was; she said he had gone to fetch some drinking water for them. The man came carrying his bucket and said, "Welcome. Nothing has visited the servants of Allah better than a Prophet who has visited me today." He hung his bucket near a palm tree, climbed it, and returned with a cluster of dates. The Prophet ﷺ asked, *"Why didn't you pick some of them?"* — and the man replied, "I wanted you to choose with your own eyes." Then he took a blade to slaughter a sheep, and the Prophet ﷺ said, *"Do not slaughter one that gives milk."* He slaughtered a sheep for them that day and they all ate.

Then the Prophet ﷺ said: *"You will be asked about this on the Day of Judgement. Hunger caused you to come out of your homes and you did not return until you had eaten this meal. So this is from the delights."* (Ibn Kathīr notes that Muslim also recorded this hadith.)

Look at what was on the table: dates and mutton, eaten by men who had left home with nothing in their stomachs. Not luxury — relief. And even that, said the Prophet ﷺ, is from *the delights* of ayah 8. If a hungry man's first meal is on the list, the modern reader may draw the obvious inference about his own.

**The two neglected favours.** Ibn Kathīr cites as confirmed in Ṣaḥīḥ Al-Bukhārī and the Sunans of At-Tirmidhī, An-Nasāʼī and Ibn Mājah, from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Two favours are treated unjustly by most people: health and free time."* Ibn Kathīr explains that this means people are lacking gratitude for these two favours, and he draws the conclusion: "whoever does not maintain the right that is obligatory upon him, then he is unjust."

That is a sharp definition. Ingratitude here is not merely bad manners; it is injustice — giving something less than its due.

**"So where is the thanks for that?"** Imām Aḥmad records from Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, will say on the Day of Judgement: *"O Son of Adam! I made you ride upon the horses and camels, I gave you women to marry, and I made you reside and rule in the earth. So where is the thanks for that?"* Ibn Kathīr notes that Aḥmad was alone in recording this hadith in this manner.

**The first question, and the five.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds two further reports. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ is reported to have said that the first question Allah will put to every person is: "Did I not give you good health, and did I not give you cold water to quench your thirst?" (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Tirmidhī and Ibn Ḥibbān, from Abū Hurayrah, as quoted by Ibn Kathīr, giving an authenticity rating for it.) And he ﷺ is also reported to have said that no man will be able to move from his place unless he answers five questions: how he spent his life; in what pursuits he expended his youthful energy; how he earned his wealth — by lawful or unlawful means; where he spent his wealth — in lawful or unlawful ways; and whether he acted upon the knowledge Allah gave him. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Bukhārī.)

Health. Cold water. A lifetime. Youth. Earning and spending. Knowledge. Between them these narrations cover almost everything a person actually has.

## Living it

The passage is not asking a believer to despise the good things of the world. In the narration of the Anṣārī's house, the Prophet ﷺ ate the dates and the mutton; he even protected the family's interest by forbidding the slaughter of the milking sheep. The favours are real and they are from Allah. What ayah 8 establishes is that they are *entrusted*, and that an accounting will be requested.

So three things follow directly from these ayat, on the reading of the commentators here:

**Let the news land now.** Ibn Kathīr's gloss on the previous ayah is that if people knew with true knowledge, rivalry for wealth would not divert them from seeking the Hereafter — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's illustration shows the gap between hearing something and seeing it. Ayat 6–7 promise that the seeing will come regardless; the only question is whether it comes while there is still time to act on it.

**Name your blessings, because they will be named.** Ibn Kathīr's list is health, safety, sustenance. Mujāhid's is food, clothes, house, wife, children, kingdom, government, honour. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the ear, the eye and the heart, from 17:36. Because the question specifies no particular blessing, as Qurṭubī observes, no blessing is off the list — including the two that pass most quietly, health and free time.

**Answer with gratitude and worship.** Ibn Kathīr frames the entire questioning around one thing: did you return His favours by being thankful to Him and worshipping Him? Gratitude in this passage is not a mood but the discharge of a right that is owed — and failing to maintain that right, in his words, is injustice.

The surah opened with people preoccupied with increase. It closes with Allah asking about everything He gave.
